chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fazzal, from Mansur, from Ammar ibn Abi al-Yaqzan, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said: 'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the right of the believer upon the believer.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'The right of the believer upon the believer is greater than that. If I were to narrate it to you, you would disbelieve. Indeed, when the believer comes out from his grave, a likeness (mithal) comes out with him from his grave, saying to him, 'Receive glad tidings of prestige from Allah and joy.' So he says to it, 'May Allah give you glad tidings of goodness.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Then it goes with him, giving him glad tidings of the like of what I said. And whenever he passes by a horror, it says, 'This is not for you'; and whenever he passes by a goodness, it says, 'This is for you'. So it does not cease to be with him, reassuring him from what he fears, and giving him glad tidings of what he likes, until it stands with him in front of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.'

So when He commands him to Paradise, the likeness says to him, 'Receive glad tidings, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has commanded you to Paradise.' He says, 'Who are you? May Allah have mercy on you. You have been giving me glad tidings from when I came out from my grave, and you comforted me on my way, and informed me about my Lord.'
He says, 'I am the Joy which you used to cause to enter upon your brethren in the world. I was created from it to give you glad tidings, and to comfort your loneliness.'
Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal — similar to it.

key_terms.السُّرُور: Joy or Gladness, personified here as a companion
key_terms.بَيْنَ يَدَيِ اللَّهِ: In front of Allah / Before Allah
key_terms.مِثَال: A spiritual likeness or form that accompanies the soul

ai.seo_question: What is the 'likeness' that accompanies a believer from the grave according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In Shia eschatology, this hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the concept of *al-Mithal* (the spiritual double) accompanying the believer from the grave, serving as a tangible manifestation of their inner state. The figure identifies itself as 'Joy' (*al-Surur*), created from the believer's own act of bringing happiness to others, thereby linking worldly social ethics directly to posthumous comfort. This narrative underscores the Shia emphasis on *ta'zir* (spiritual companionship) and the continuity of personal agency in the afterlife.
